profile.address: 32 Avenue of the Americas, Tribeca, New York, NY 10013
profile.reading:
32 Avenue of the Americas, also known as 32 Sixth Avenue, is a 27 story, 1.17 million square foot office tower in Manhattan's Tribeca neighborhood, at the border of SoHo. It was designed by architect Ralph Thomas Walker of the firm Voorhees, Gmelin and Walker and built in stages. An initial Walker Lispenard Building went up in 1914 and was expanded in 1919, with a final major expansion between 1929 and 1932 producing the building's current Art Deco form. It was constructed as the AT&T Long Lines Building, the switching point for AT&T's long distance network. At its peak, every Bell System trunk line in the northeastern United States converged inside the building, linking 360 cities across roughly three thousand direct lines, and the building also carried radio circuits, teletype service, and photo transmission links to other major American cities.

The building's landmarked facade and lobby, including its mosaic murals, were designated a New York City landmark on October 1, 1991. Rudin Management Company acquired the property in 1999 and hired Fox and Fowle Architects for a modernization completed in 2002 that adapted the historic tower for contemporary office and telecommunications tenants while preserving its protected exterior and lobby.

That AT&T heritage carried directly into the building's present use. The 24th floor houses The Hub, a carrier neutral colocation and interconnection facility that Rudin markets as a meeting point for buyers and sellers of network capacity, serving more than 50 terrestrial carriers, content providers, internet service providers, and enterprise tenants. Rudin's own marketing for the building describes floor plates ranging from about 25,000 to 52,000 square feet, heavy floor loading capacity suited to telecom and technical equipment, and abundant power, cooling, and generator capacity. The building uses the Nantum operating system for real time building management and has earned WiredScore Platinum certification, a rating specifically aimed at telecom and connectivity readiness in commercial buildings.

No public source breaks out a megawatt figure for The Hub specifically, since it occupies one floor within a much larger mixed use office tower rather than standing as a purpose built, single tenant data center. What is published, consistently across the building's owner and independent accounts of its history, is that this is one of the most consequential pieces of telecommunications real estate in the country. It is a former Bell System nerve center whose landmark status protects its exterior even as its interior continues to function as a working interconnection point for the internet era, a rare case where a building's original telecommunications purpose and its current one are directly continuous rather than a later repurposing of unrelated space.

reading.body:
The Hub occupies a single floor of a 1.17 million square foot Manhattan office building originally constructed for AT&T between 1914 and 1932. It functions as a carrier-neutral colocation and interconnection point serving over 50 network operators, content providers, and enterprise customers. No power capacity is published for the facility.

New York has only one data center with published power specifications in this database, totaling 3 MW. This campus ranks second by published capacity in the state, though that ranking reflects the absence of published figures rather than measured scale. The state has 31 mapped facilities overall, the vast majority of which disclose no power draw.

The facility qualifies for colocation and terrestrial carrier interconnection. Whether the Hub's IT load can support meaningful AI workloads depends on figures not published, including floor-level power allocation, cooling capacity, and current occupancy. Tribeca location and landmark designation impose constraints on physical expansion that are not quantified here.
